title: Bobby Deol Just Delivered the Performance of His Career. Bollywood Almost Didn't Notice.
excerpt: Anurag Kashyap's Bandar opened to empty seats and four-star reviews. Three days later, the evening shows are packed.
body:
Bobby Deol walked into a room full of people who had already made up their minds about him, and by the time the lights came up, not one of them was thinking about **Animal** anymore.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=4E0-K9F16r8</youtube>

**Bandar**, Anurag Kashyap's gritty crime thriller, opened on June 5 to a half-empty theatre in most cities. The multiplex chains had given it the leftovers — 3 PM slots, back screens, whatever Varun Dhawan's **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai** and Ram Charan's **Peddi** didn't need. By Saturday evening, those same screens were full. By Sunday, they were packed.

The numbers tell one story. Opening day: ₹0.50 crore across barely 555 shows. Day 2: ₹0.95 crore — a 90% jump. By the weekend, evening and night shows were reporting housefull boards across metros. The growth hasn't come from spectacle. It's come from people texting their friends.

> "You can't stop anyone. Every producer thinks, 'Why should I move?' But for *Bandar*, the strategy was never about a massive opening. It was about a long run." — Trade veteran Taran Adarsh

## The Performance Everyone Is Talking About

**Bobby Deol** plays Samar, a singer-actor whose career is in freefall. When a woman named Gayatri (**Sapna Pabbi**) files a rape complaint against him, his life becomes a legal circus — and the film becomes something far more uncomfortable than a courtroom drama. Written by **Sudip Sharma** and **Abhishek Banerjee**, it is based on a real-life incident, though the film never names it. It doesn't need to.

What's remarkable is the restraint. Bobby — who spent the last two years playing broad, menacing heavies in **Animal** and **Alpha** — dials everything down. He's wounded, disoriented, too proud to ask for help and too broken to refuse it. Critics across publications have given the film four stars or above. Several are calling it the best-reviewed Hindi release of the year.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYwOe8-tX1r/

Kashyap's direction deserves equal credit. This is the filmmaker who made **Gangs of Wasseypur** feel like a lived-in world, and he does the same here — the police stations feel grimy, the courtrooms feel exhausting, the media circus feels sickeningly familiar. He maintains tension while letting the film's moral ambiguities breathe. There are no heroes. There are no easy answers.

## The Screen War Behind the Scenes

The most Bollywood part of this story happened off-screen. **Zee Studios**, the film's producer, put the multiplex release on hold when national chains offered Bandar scraps. Their ask was modest — 3-4 shows per multiplex after 1 PM, on 500-600 screens. But with PVR, Inox, and Cinepolis distributing the competing films directly, Bandar got squeezed.

Zee's distribution head **Girish Johar** didn't blink. He held the programming until a fair deal was struck. The gamble was simple: this film doesn't need a massive opening. It needs enough screens for word-of-mouth to do the work.

That gamble is paying off. In an industry addicted to ₹100-crore opening days, Bandar is proving that conviction still has a box office. The film hasn't crossed ₹2 crore in a single day — and it doesn't need to. The conversation around it is louder than any of its competitors.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

Bandar is a limited release internationally, but it's screening in select theatres across the US, UK, and Canada. For diaspora audiences who've watched Bobby Deol evolve from the pretty boy of the '90s to the scene-stealing villain of **Animal**, this is the next chapter — and arguably the most interesting one. He's not playing a type. He's playing a person.

If your local theatre is showing it, go. If it's not, demand it. This is the kind of film that makes you remember why you go to the movies in the first place — not for the spectacle, but for the silence after the lights come up when nobody knows what to say.
